'''Germaine Cohen-Bazire Stanier''' (2 September 1920 – 9 May 2001) was a French microbiologist. A 1960 [[Guggenheim Fellow]], she studied the role of proteins and other chemicals in the biological processes of bacteria. She worked as a researcher at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] and [[Pasteur Institute]], the latter of where she chaired the Unité de Physiologie Microbienne.

==Biography==
Germaine Bazire was born on 2 September 1920 in [[Thonon-les-Bains]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Institut Pasteur {{!}} Archives |url=https://webext.pasteur.fr/archives/cbg0.html |access-date=2026-04-01 |website=webext.pasteur.fr}}</ref> Her mother taught at a primary school and her father taught science at a secondary school.<ref name="ASM 2001"/> She obtained a ''[[baccalauréat]]'' at a Toulouse lycée in 1938 and moved onto the [[University of Toulouse]], a ''licence ès sciences'' in 1942 and ''diplôme d'études supérieures'' in 1945.<ref name="GF"/>

She joined the [[French National Centre for Scientific Research]] in 1945, serving as a research chief from 1955 to 1957.<ref name="GF"/> During this period, she obtained her ScD from the [[University of Paris]] in 1950,<ref name="GF"/> with her thesis involving her research on [[butyric]] and [[acetonobutylic]] fermentation, supervised by Georges Cohen.<ref name="ASM 2001"/> She also worked at [[Jacques Monod]]'s laboratory at the [[Pasteur Institute]].<ref name="ASM 2001"/> In 1953, she moved to the [[University of California, Berkeley]] as a postdoctoral fellow, starting as a junior research bacteriologist before becoming a research bacteriologist in 1956.<ref name="GF"/><ref name="Govindjee 2004"/>

During her early career at the Pasteur Institute, she researched enzyme induction and in 1953, helped discover what represses the ability of [[tryptophan]] to produce [[tryptophan synthase]].<ref name="ASM 2001"/> She started researching [[alphaproteobacteria]] and [[cyanobacteria]] while working at UCB, including [[athiorhodaceae]] and [[chloroniums]], and she once studied the role of [[phycobiliprotein]]s in cyanobacteria.<ref name="ASM 2001"/> She also isolated a mutated strain of [[cereibacter sphaeroides]] to further advance research on [[carotenoid]]s.<ref name="ASM 2001"/>

She appeared at the 1959 [[Oregon State University]] Biology Colloquium along with several nationally-known biologists.<ref>{{cite news |date=1969-04-22 |title=Biology Colloquium At OSU To Attract Top U.S. Scientistsp |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/384034240/ |work=Corvallis Gazette-Times |page=18 |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> In 1960, she was awarded a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]] to study the "regulation of the synthesis of structural units in bacterial cells".<ref>{{cite news |date=1960-04-25 |title=Guggenheims to 23 Berkeleyans |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/994313045/ |work=The Berkeley Gazette |page=11 |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> ''[[Photosynthesis Research]]'' called her a "world leader in the ultrastructure and physiology of cyanobacteria",<ref name="Govindjee 2004"/> while a trio of Pasteur Institute colleagues – [[Agnes Ullmann]], Georges N. Cohen, and [[François Jacob]] – renarked that she was "internationally recognized as one of the specialists on photosynthetic prokaryotes".<ref name="ASM 2001"/>

Returning from the United States, she rejoined the Pasteur Institute in 1971.<ref name="Govindjee 2004"/> She was appointed head of the Unité de Physiologie Microbienne in 1982 and professor at the Pasteur Institute in 1985, before she retired from the institution in 1988.<ref name="Govindjee 2004"/><ref name="ASM 2001"/> She served as the treasurer of the [[International Cell Research Organization]].<ref name="ASM 2001"/>

Her second marriage was to [[Roger Stanier]], a Canadian microbiologist with whom she worked at the Pasteur Institute.<ref name="Govindjee 2004"/> They had one daughter, as well as a son from a previous marriage.<ref name="ASM 2001"/> She cited [[André Michel Lwoff]] and [[Jacques Monod]], both Nobel laureates, as her "guardian angel" and "master of thinking" respectively.<ref name="ASM 2001"/> She died on 9 May 2001 in Vancouver, where she had retired in the last eight years; she was 80.<ref name="ASM 2001"/><ref>{{Cite news |date=May 17, 2001 |title=STANIER |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-vancouver-sun-obituary-for-germaine/70384856/ |access-date=2026-04-01 |work=The Vancouver Sun |pages=F13}}</ref>
